abstract.t: Status: proposed. Module: std/crypto/scram.ts (nish/crypto/scram). The key derivation and proofs a SCRAM-SHA-256 client computes (RFC 5802 Section 3, with SHA-256 as RFC 7677 Section 3 sets it): SaltedPassword from the password, salt and iteration count, then ClientProof and ServerSignature from SaltedPassword and the AuthMessage. nish/net/postgres authenticates with them.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

The module holds the arithmetic of SCRAM-SHA-256 and nothing of its messages: the caller builds AuthMessage, decodes the server's base64 salt and encodes the proof. The password reaches it as Secret bytes already normalized; Normalize, SASLprep in RFC 5802, is the caller's, and nish/net/postgres sends the password's UTF-8 bytes unchanged, as a PostgreSQL server accepts.

RFC 7677 Section 3 prints one SCRAM-SHA-256 exchange, as base64 inside wrapped protocol messages. vector binds a printed string to a value only whole and only beside the other values on its line, so the exchange cannot be cited value by value. Each vector below therefore takes its expected value from a command that spec check --run-sources runs: Python's hashlib for SaltedPassword, which the exchange does not print, and a base64 decode of the printed p= and v= for ClientProof and ServerSignature, so those two are the RFC's own values.

The arguments are the exchange's: the password 'pencil', the salt the server sends as s=W22ZaJ0SNY7soEsUEjb6gQ== (the 16 bytes [5b 6d 99 68 9d 12 35 8e ec a0 4b 14 12 36 fa 81]), the iteration count 4096, and the AuthMessage that S2 and S3 pass: RFC 5802 Section 3 joins the client-first message without its n,, header, the server-first message and the client-final message without its proof, with a comma between each.

section.name: Interface
section.sourcecode: // module: nish/crypto/scram export const scramSha256SaltedPassword = (password: Secret<u8[]>, salt: u8[], iterations: i32): Secret<u8[]> | null export const scramSha256ClientProof = (saltedPassword: Secret<u8[]>, authMessage: u8[]): u8[] export const scramSha256ServerSignature = (saltedPassword: Secret<u8[]>, authMessage: u8[]): u8[]

blockquote.t: the hash function for HMAC() and H() uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1 [RFC6234].
Hi() is, essentially, PBKDF2 [RFC2898] with HMAC() as the pseudorandom function (PRF) and with dkLen == output length of HMAC() == output length of H().

section.name: A refused count
section.t: Hi takes at least one round, U1. scramSha256SaltedPassword MUST return null when the iteration count is less than 1.

blockquote.t: ClientSignature := HMAC(StoredKey, AuthMessage) ClientProof := ClientKey XOR ClientSignature
ServerKey := HMAC(SaltedPassword, "Server Key") ServerSignature := HMAC(ServerKey, AuthMessage)

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: SaltedPassword, ClientKey and ServerKey each let whoever holds them authenticate as the user, so the module takes and gives SaltedPassword as a Secret and wipes ClientKey, StoredKey, ClientSignature and ServerKey before it returns. ClientProof and ServerSignature are sent in the clear and are plain bytes. A caller compares a server's signature with timingSafeEqual. The iteration count is the server's to choose: a caller caps it, since Hi runs that many HMACs. No returned value shows the wipes, so no vector here tests them; the module's security record does.

front.title: Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) SASL and GSS-API Mechanisms

abstract.t: The secure authentication mechanism most widely deployed and used by Internet application protocols is the transmission of clear-text passwords over a channel protected by Transport Layer Security (TLS). There are some significant security concerns with that mechanism, which could be addressed by the use of a challenge response authentication mechanism protected by TLS. Unfortunately, the challenge response mechanisms presently on the standards track all fail to meet requirements necessary for widespread deployment, and have had success only in limited use.

This specification describes a family of Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL; RFC 4422) authentication mechanisms called the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM), which addresses the security concerns and meets the deployability requirements. When used in combination with TLS or an equivalent security layer, a mechanism from this family could improve the status quo for application protocol authentication and provide a suitable choice for a mandatory-to-implement mechanism for future application protocol standards. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Mechanisms

abstract.t: This document registers the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) mechanisms SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, provides guidance for secure implementation of the original SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS mechanism, and updates the SCRAM registration procedures of RFC 5802.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
